questions.question: should I treat my boots out of box ? Annnnd how often should I treat them ?

hybrid.answer:
It depends on the boot, and my experience is with Blundstones. Most Blundstones come pretreated, and Blundstone itself doesn't recommend treating them out of the box [1]. The exception is the rustic or distressed leathers, which don't carry the same pretreatment [2]. For those I strongly recommend conditioning them [3].

**How often:** I treat mine when they seem to need it, not on a fixed schedule. It depends on how much you wear them and where you go [4]. Signs it's time are leather that looks or feels dry, or water no longer beading on top. Dryness means more oil or wax, and dirty boots need cleaning [4]. Earlier I said you might have to wax every month, or even every week if you're hard on them [5]. Now I go by feel.

**Process:** Clean the boots first, because treating over dirt makes a mess [6]. Then go in order: clean, condition, wax [7].

I haven't covered other kinds of boots, so this applies to Blundstones.

questions.question: So if I buy the levis 501 shrink to fit will they get tighter after washing?

hybrid.answer:
Yes. The first soak or wash tightens them, mostly in the waist, and I'd size up to allow for that.

- **How much:** All the 501s I compared are unsanforized, so they can shrink up to 10% the first time you wash them [1].
- **Where it shows:** When I shrank mine, they slimmed up mainly around the waist [2]. The length barely changed [3].
- **Heat and the dryer:** Hot water and the dryer make them smaller. My shrunk pair looked much better because I didn't use very hot water or the dryer, so don't put yours in the dryer or rinse them that hot [4].
- **Sizing:** I'd usually go two sizes up [5]. When I didn't size up, I could barely pull on my 29 waist at first and couldn't breathe [6].
- **After wearing them:** They loosen with wear. After a week the waist had stretched enough for a belt [7]. After a year of wear, the fit was really good for me [8].

questions.question: I'm usually a 33x30 in Levi's 502s, what size should I buy in these? [501 STF]

hybrid.answer:
I'd go with a 35 waist and a 32 length. My rule for the 501 STF is to size up two in the waist and get two inches more in length, so your 33x30 becomes 35x32 [1][2].

**Why:** They shrink when you soak them. If you follow that rule, the pants fit normally once they're wet [2].

**What happened when I ignored it:** I bought a 29x30 and could barely pull them on and couldn't breathe. The waist did loosen with wear, and they ended up a good fit [3]. The length was the miss: I'd have gotten a 32 [3].

**What I haven't covered:** I haven't talked about how the 502 fits compared with the 501. I've only applied my 501 STF sizing rule to the size you gave me.

questions.question: Why do you cuff your jeans?

hybrid.answer:
I cuff mainly because I can't settle on one hem length. I can never decide between no break, half break or full break, and cuffing is the only fix I've found short of committing to one length [1]. I also cuffed my 501s because my current style doesn't suit wider-legged pants worn uncuffed [2]. In that case the cuff also covered for the length: I'd have gotten a 32 [2].

How I cuff depends on the boots. I used to cuff all the time, but with boots I now like the jeans worn down over them, which calms the boots down [3].

questions.question: So do you prefer [the Red Wing 3335s] over the 1907s?

hybrid.answer:
Mostly yes, I've favored the 3335s over the 1907s, but I've since hedged. I've said the 3335s are my favorite Red Wings of all time, and they still might be, but they're probably not [the 875s, 1907s and Iron Rangers each have characteristics I really like](cite). I'm also letting the 3335s go from my collection [2].

**Why I liked the 3335s more:** They're my favorite boots I've ever had, and they beat my Blundstones, the 1907s and the 875s [3]. I'm not doing heritage work. I'm hiking and walking in the woods, and for that they're a much better all-around boot [3]. They're stitch-down, lighter and more nimble, and easier to go walking in [1].

**Where the 1907s win:** The 1907s and 875s are more beefily constructed, so if you need a tough boot, the 3335s are probably not the ones to go for [3]. Among moc toe Red Wings, I think you should get the 1907s [4].

questions.question: How do you feel bout blunnies as of Late 2023?

hybrid.answer:
I'm a big fan of Blundstones and have always loved them, even though some people don't like them [1]. My 585s, which I've worn constantly, have held up and stayed my most water resistant boots [1]. I'm retiring that heavily worn pair, though [1].

I also keep Blundstone-style slip-ons for quick errands or rain. They are shoes I can flop on in any weather, though I could easily put them on the sell list [2]. The heavy-duty Blundstone 989 Extreme is going. I thought it was waterproof, but it's only very water-resistant nubuck [3].

My view has stayed fairly consistent over time. After a year, they performed as I'd hoped for the price, and I expected them to look pretty good for several years [4]. At the start I recommended them as long as you keep them treated, and I called them my favourite boots of the few I owned [5][6].

questions.question: How does the made in England boot stack up to Solovairs? [Dr. Martens]

hybrid.answer:
Solovair comes out ahead for me. It's a better boot that costs less, with no Doc Martens markup [1][2]. The one reason to pick the Made in England Docs is if you're a big Dr. Martens fan.

**Price and value:** Solovair is about $40 cheaper than the Made in England Docs [2]. On the extra $90 for the England boots over the Thailand ones, my answer is probably not worth it [3]. You have to be a mega fan to get them [4].

**Leather and midsole:** The England boots' leather is better and should age fine, roughly on par with Solovair [5]. Solovair does use full grain leather [6]. The midsoles are thicker, heavier and more robust on Solovair [7].

**Comfort and repair:** Solovairs have a shank, which makes them more comfortable over long periods [8]. Docs don't have one [9]. Solovair also sells its soles on its website, so the boots are easier to resole and last longer [10].

**Where Made in England wins:** If you want the yellow stitching, you have to get the Made in England Docs [11]. And if you're a huge fan who wants something close to how old Docs were made, they're the only choice [12].

**Solovair's downside:** My pairs had quality-control problems, but I think those were isolated. My only real gripe is the laces possibly fraying on the eyelets [13].

questions.question: Hi, I am going on a 4 day hike and I am wondering if I can use my blundstone for them, what do you think?

hybrid.answer:
I wouldn't pick them for a 4-day hike if you have a better option. They lack good ankle support, so they aren't good boots for mountain hiking [1]. That said, I took mine up and down a few mountains in Maine and they held up well, with some scuffing [2]. I haven't tested them on a multi-day trek, so I can't say how they'd do over four days.

**Break-in:** Make sure they're properly broken in first. I got big break-in blisters once I started running and walking a track in mine, and they only stopped after two to three weeks [3].

**Other boots:** For long hikes, I like the padding on my Jim Green Razorbacks [4]. I also have Hoka hiking boots, my first modern, maximalist hiking boots, but I hadn't finished testing them for hiking [5].

questions.question: I'm 5'11-225 lbs with a dad bod. What's the most cost efficient and quality t shirt for me? Also, what size would u prefer?

hybrid.answer:
I'd go for the Muji t-shirt. My rule is that Uniqlo is the best t-shirt you can get for the price at $20 [1], but if you're taller or wider, you'd want Muji [2]. At 5'11" and 225 lbs, I'd put you in that group. Muji costs about $4 or $5 more, but it's significantly longer and a good deal wider [3].

**Why Muji over Uniqlo:** Earlier I said the Muji is about $10 more and that the extra money felt justified, because the shirt feels better and the collar is a little thicker and tighter [4]. Uniqlo is still a great starter shirt with a bound collar that doesn't wiggle [5].

**Other options:** If you want a bit more money in the mix, the Front General Store is $40 and made in Japan [6]. House of Blanks is $35 and made in Canada with zero torque [7]. I also said the Los Angeles Apparel tee might win if you size down one [8].

**Size:** I haven't given a specific size recommendation for your build in my videos, so I can't say which size I'd pick for you.

questions.question: Hi, what are some fall/winter sneakers you'd recommend?

hybrid.answer:
The sneaker I'd point you to for colder, wetter months is the Samara, my collaboration with Goral Footwear. These are my favorite hiking shoes around [1]. The leather is Charles F Stead Waxy Commander, which is highly water resistant [2]. The outsole is Vibram Arctic Grip, which is meant to increase slip resistance on wet ice [3]. It also has a lug that turns blue when temperatures fall below freezing, to warn you of ice [3]. It's my own collaboration product, so weigh that accordingly.

**Feit Classic Low:** These are my favorite sneakers, and I wear them every day [4]. I haven't singled them out as a fall or winter pick, though.

I haven't made a ranked list of fall and winter sneakers beyond that.

questions.question: 1907 vs the 875's? What's the difference?

hybrid.answer:
I'd go for the 1907 if you're looking at a Red Wing moc toe, and I think it's the better pick over the 875 [1]. The main difference is construction: the 875 is Goodyear welted, while the 1907 has a storm (Norwegian-like) welt [2][3].

**Welt and water:** The 875's Goodyear welt is durable and fairly water resistant, and it leaves room for a cork footbed that molds to your foot [3]. The 1907's storm welt is something I find invaluable [4]. From what I've read, Red Wing's version is probably just an extra strip of leather stitched onto the welt, which is said to have a similar effect to a true storm welt, though I'm not quite sure [5]. In my standing-in-water test, one 1907 leaked almost immediately through the stitching and the other stayed dry. I'd still expect them to hold up fine in rain, grass or mud [6]. Leather welted boots like these aren't really strong on water resistance, so for heavy rain or slush I prefer Blundstones [7].

**Price and extras:** The 1907 costs about $10 more, but it comes with a removable leather footbed (usually around $40 separately) and leather laces (usually around $15) [4]. That's why I see it as the better deal [8].

**Soles:** Both the 875 and 1907 have crepe soles, which I don't love and which I expect to break down faster than the Vibram mini lug on the 3335 [1][9].

**Build:** Both are the beefier heritage-style boots, so they suit you better if you need a tough boot [10].

questions.question: How does Uniqlo compare to The Front General Store,  Proclub, and Hanes? ie what is the best budget shirt?

hybrid.answer:
**Uniqlo is the best budget shirt on price alone.** At about $20 it is probably the best t-shirt you can get for the money [1]. I'd call it a starter tee, though it's open-ended and a bit rough [2]. It also has a bound neck collar that doesn't wiggle [3].

**Front General Store:** At $40 it costs twice as much, but it's my pick in the affordable, best-value category. It's 100% made in Japan, with great proportions and a great feel [4]. I'm favouring it right now [5]. It uses open-end yarn, sanded for some softness [6]. It scored 6 out of 10 for softness [7].

**Hanes:** It's a classic $10 shirt, and a great one [8]. It's much softer than Pro Club [9], and I gave it 7 out of 10 for softness [8]. It shrank 6.73% in length [10].

**Pro Club:** I like it, but it's the roughest shirt in that test [11]. It scored 4 out of 10 for softness [11].

I haven't compared Uniqlo directly against Hanes or Pro Club in my videos. For Uniqlo's own numbers, the heavyweight crew shrank 2.3% in width and 2% in length [12].

questions.question: Would you recommend this [Barbour Bedale] or the flint and tinder for someone who would use it like a rain jacket but also a windbreaker and a spring light jacket?

hybrid.answer:
I'd lean toward the Bedale for that mix of uses, though I haven't compared the two on rain or wind directly. A few points on each:

**Bedale**
- **Spring weight:** The Barbour fabric is the lightest of the waxed jackets I looked at, and you can wear it any time of year over or under different layers [1].
- **Rain:** With a fresh coat of wax it didn't leak at all in my shower test. It isn't waterproof, but it is very water resistant when properly treated [2]. Once the wax wears down, it won't be nearly as water resistant [3].
- **Rain features:** I'd get the snap-on hood [4]. The Bedale also has a storm flap over the zipper [5].
- **Wind:** The tighter-woven thornproof finish adds wind resistance [6].
- **Caveat:** It's not a designated rain jacket [7].

**Flint and Tinder Waxed Trucker**
- **Fit and weight:** I'd say it suits everyone. It's a lighter weight, so it's comfortable, though not crazy lightweight [8]. It's lined, so you don't get wax on your skin [9].
- **Price:** It's $300 for a lined, US-made waxed jacket, and I don't see an obvious sacrifice in it [9].
- **Sponsorship:** That video was sponsored by Huckberry, though I'd talked about this jacket many times before [10].
- **Not covered:** I haven't tested it in rain or talked about its wind resistance, so I can't rank it against the Bedale on those.

questions.question: Great video. But just curious, how can you say it's a con that the Huckberry jacket is unlined when they sell two different versions of lined waxed truckers: wool, and flannel?

hybrid.answer:
The con was about the unlined version of the Huckberry jacket, which is the one I was reviewing in that video. It isn't a knock on the lined versions. The jacket I showed was the cheapest, simplest, unlined one on the list [1], and I did say it's a little more cropped than the lined version [2]. My gripe is that I always like a lining in a waxed jacket so the wax isn't touching your clothes or arms [3]. That applied to the unlined Huckberry and Rogue Territory jackets [3].

The lined flannel version is the one I recommend. It's lined, so you don't get wax on your skin [4]. I also like that Huckberry sells an unlined version for people who want one [5]. I haven't tried the wool-lined one yet, but I think it's a really nice jacket [6].

My view on unlined jackets has softened a bit. I usually still want a liner, but I now see why you might leave a jacket unlined [7].

questions.question: Do you know how these fit compared to the 875s? [Red Wing 3335s]

hybrid.answer:
I haven't directly compared the fit of the 3335s to the 875s in my videos. What I can say is that I went true to size in the 3335s and they fit fine [1]. They have a slim profile and taper down, and with wool socks my toes feel squished and I can't wiggle them much. With thin cotton socks in warm weather I had no tightness [1].

The closest thing on the 875 side is that the 875 and 1907 are more beefily constructed than the 3335 [2]. That is about build, not fit. When I bought Red Wings in my usual boot size, they fit perfectly [3]. That was the 1907 video, not the 875 or 3335. My general rule for Red Wings and most leather boots is to buy them snug but not squished [3].
